question.text: \[ A=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad D = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 6 \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $D=P^T \! AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the third column of the matrix $P?$
question.explanation:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

\[ A=PDP^T, \] where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

\[ D=P^TAP. \]

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D=P^T \! AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are $\lambda_1=0,$ $\lambda_2=-2,$ and $\lambda_3=6.$ So, the third column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_3=6.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda_3=6.$ Computing $A-6I,$ we get

\begin{align*} A - 6 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} - 6 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -5 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & -4 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & -5 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector

\[ \mathbf{v}_3 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \]

where $\| \mathbf{v}_3 \| = \sqrt{3}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_3$ by its norm, we obtain the third column of $P\mathbin{:}$ \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_3}{\|\mathbf{v}_3\|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \\ \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \\ \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \end{bmatrix} \]

question.text: \[ A=\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 3 & 3 \\ 3 & -1 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad D = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 8 \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $D=P^T \! AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the second column of the matrix $P?$
question.explanation:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

\[ A=PDP^T, \] where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

\[ D=P^TAP. \]

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D=P^T \! AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are $\lambda_1=-3,$ $\lambda_2=0,$ and $\lambda_3=8.$ So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_2=0.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda_2=0.$ Computing $A-0I,$ we get

\begin{align*} A - 0 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 3 & 3 \\ 3 & -1 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 3 \end{bmatrix} - 0 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 3 & 3 \\ 3 & -1 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 3 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector

\[ \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \]

where $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{2}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm, we obtain the second column of $P\mathbin{:}$ \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2}{\|\mathbf{v}_2\|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0 \\ \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \end{bmatrix} \]

question.text: \[ A=\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 3 & 3 \\ 3 & -1 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad D = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 8 \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $D=P^T \! AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the third column of the matrix $P?$
question.explanation:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

\[ A=PDP^T, \] where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

\[ D=P^TAP. \]

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D=P^T \! AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are $\lambda_1=-3,$ $\lambda_2=0,$ and $\lambda_3=8.$ So, the third column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_3=8.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda_3=8.$ Computing $A-8I,$ we get

\begin{align*} A - 8 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 3 & 3 \\ 3 & -1 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 3 \end{bmatrix} - 8 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -5 & 3 & 3 \\ 3 & -9 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & -5 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-8I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector

\[ \mathbf{v}_3 = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}, \]

where $\| \mathbf{v}_3 \| = \sqrt{22}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_3$ by its norm, we obtain the third column of $P\mathbin{:}$ \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_3}{\|\mathbf{v}_3\|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{22}} \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{22}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{22}} \\ \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{22}} \end{bmatrix} \]

question.text: \[ A=\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 8 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad D = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 9 \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $D=P^T \! AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first and second columns of the matrix $P?$
question.explanation:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

\[ A=PDP^T, \] where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

\[ D=P^TAP. \]

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D=P^T \! AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=4,$ and $\lambda_3=9.$ So, the first and second columns of $P$ correspond to the eigenvalues $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2. $

Now, we need to find eigenvectors that correspond to $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=4.$ Computing $A-4I,$ we get

\begin{align*} A - 4 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 8 \end{bmatrix} - 4 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives two eigenvectors:

$\qquad$ $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \quad$ and $\quad \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$

Notice that eigenvectors $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$ are orthogonal. Finally, dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$ by their respective norms, we obtain the first and second columns of $P\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1}{\|\mathbf{v}_1\|} &= \dfrac{1}{1} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\0\\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\[10pt] \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2}{\|\mathbf{v}_2\|} &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{{5}}} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ \dfrac{2\sqrt{5}}{5} \\ \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{5} \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

question.text: \[ A=\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad D = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 7 \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $D=P^T \! AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first and second columns of the matrix $P?$
question.explanation:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

\[ A=PDP^T, \] where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

\[ D=P^TAP. \]

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D=P^T \! AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are $\lambda_1=1,$ $\lambda_2=1,$ and $\lambda_3=7.$ So, the first and second columns of $P$ correspond to the eigenvalue $\lambda_1=1.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=1.$ Computing $A-I,$ we get

\begin{align*} A - I &= \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives two eigenvectors:

$\qquad$ $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \quad$ and $\quad \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$

Notice that eigenvectors $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$ are not orthogonal. So, we proceed using the Gram-Schmidt process. We set \[ \mathbf{e}_1=\mathbf{v}_1=\begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \] and we find $\mathbf{e}_2$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{e}_2 &= \mathbf{v}_2 - \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 \cdot \mathbf{e}_1}{\mathbf{e}_1 \cdot \mathbf{e}_1}\mathbf{e}_1 \\[5pt] &= \mathbf{v}_2 - \dfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{e}_1 \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} - \dfrac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{2}\\ 1\\ -\dfrac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Finally, dividing $\mathbf{e}_1$ and $\mathbf{e}_2$ by their respective norms, we obtain the first and second columns of $P\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\mathbf{e}_1}{\|\mathbf{e}_1\|} &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0 \\ \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \end{bmatrix} \\[10pt] \dfrac{\mathbf{e}_2}{\|\mathbf{e}_2\|} &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}} \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{2} \\ 1 \\ -\dfrac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{6} \\ \dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{3} \\ -\dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{6} \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}
